history.text: Hi, yeah, thanks for having me. Um, I guess I’ll just say I’m really interested in software engineering because I like solving problems, you know? I had this internship where I worked on a React dashboard, so that was pretty cool. I sort of got to apply what I learned in class, like, building stuff.

Great! Now let's talk about your hands-on experience with these topics. 

Marcus, can you share more about your experience with data structures? What specific data structures have you worked with, and in what context?

Oh, um, yeah, so I’ve, like, mostly worked with basic data structures from my coursework. I, um, I’m familiar with arrays and, like, linked lists and, um, dictionaries in Python. In our chess engine project, we used some of these to, like, keep track of the game state and moves. But, uh, I wouldn’t say I’ve, like, implemented anything super complex yet.

Great! Now let's talk about your hands-on experience with these topics.

Have you had any experience working with REST APIs, Marcus? If so, could you describe a project where you utilized them and any challenges you faced during that process?

Um, so, I guess I don’t have, like, a ton of experience with REST APIs specifically. But in my Flask todo app project, we, like, created some endpoints to manage tasks. It was, um, a bit tricky to figure out the routing and, like, how to handle the data responses. I think, like, testing those endpoints was a challenge too, um, but I learned a lot from it.

Great! Now that we've discussed your hands-on experience, let's move on to some technical concepts. 

Marcus, can you explain the differences between arrays and linked lists? In what scenarios might you choose one over the other?

Oh, um, sure! So, I guess, like, arrays are, um, contiguous blocks of memory, and they have a fixed size, right? So, accessing elements is pretty fast, like, O(1) time, I think. But, um, inserting or deleting elements can be slow because you might need to shift stuff around. 

Linked lists, on the other hand, are, like, collections of nodes, and they can grow or shrink dynamically. Inserting or deleting is easier because you just, um, change the pointers, but accessing elements is slower, like O(n), I believe. 

I guess if you know the size ahead of time, you might go with arrays, but if you need a lot of inserts and deletes, linked lists could be better?

Let's dive into some technical concepts. We'll start with another question about data structures.

Marcus, can you explain how hash tables work at a high level? What are their key advantages and disadvantages?

Um, okay, so, like, hash tables store key-value pairs, right? They use a hash function to, um, map keys to specific indices in an array, which makes looking up values really fast, like O(1) on average, I think. 

But, um, one disadvantage is that if there are, like, many collisions, where different keys end up in the same index, it can slow things down. Also, um, resizing the table can be a bit costly if it gets too full. So, yeah, those are, like, some key points about hash tables, I guess.
Thank you, Marcus Lee. That covers our technical discussion. It was great to learn about your experiences and insights on these concepts. We appreciate your time and enthusiasm today!

Oh, um, thank you so much! I really appreciate the opportunity to, like, talk about my experiences. It was, um, great to share what I know, and I’m, like, really excited about the possibility of, you know, working with your team. Thanks again for, um, having me!

You're very welcome, Marcus! Thank you for sharing your experiences and insights with us. It was a pleasure speaking with you, and we appreciate your enthusiasm for the role.
